Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for writing OMIM phenotype entries with one LLM (Claude Opus 5.5) from exactly the papers the curators cited: 100 entries with 2-12 references, 515 papers, of which 19% are readable in full via open access (Sec. 3.1). Only the generation strategy varies. The strategies are direct reading (all papers in one prompt), an agentic curator, an evidence graph, a case table, recall-then-verify, a memory-only control and three add-ons. All drafts pass through the same guards and the same claim-level audit with one repair round (Sec. 3.2-3.3). The primary endpoint, 'OMIM facts conveyed', is the coverage of 6,652 atomic facts split once from OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs deposited in ClinVar. It is judged per cited paper, with half credit for partial matches, by the same model family. Main findings: (1) hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (+43.7 points, 95% CI 38.3-49.1; 46 entries; Fig. 2a, Table 24). (2) On the 93 entries every strategy completed, the agent and the evidence graph are within about 0.6 points of direct reading, and the case table trails by 1.9 points (-3.1 to -0.8, sign test p=0.071) (Table 1). The order depends on the entry set and on extraction settings (post hoc ablation, Table 21). (3) Conditional on the supplied text stating a fact, the reading strategies convey 91-94% of facts, against 5.5-6.9% of facts it does not state (Table 19). (4) On 38 held-out entries a completeness pass adds 2.6 points (1.7-3.6) but lengthens drafts by about a third (Tables 30, 34). (5) Planted-error tests show that the audit catches citation swaps and blunt value substitutions. It misses added irrelevant citations, because a claim takes the best verdict over its cited papers, and it cannot see omissions (Fig. 4, Tables 50-52). Released pipelines (PaperQA2, GraphRAG, STORM), input padding, large entries and 2026-created entries are reported as exploratory (Sec. 4.4, App. J, K, M).
Strengths: Careful control of confounds that most system comparisons leave open. Model, sources, guards, audit and scoring are held fixed and only the strategy varies (Fig. 1, Sec. 3.2). The access manipulation is within-paper (the same papers with and without full text), which turns an otherwise observational access effect (Tables 13-14) into a clean paired comparison (Table 24).

Statistical reporting is thorough and honest. It includes paired bootstrap intervals over entries, better/worse/tied counts, exact sign tests with Holm adjustment for secondary measures (Tables 7-8), run-to-run replicates and judge re-runs that give a noise yardstick (App. E, Table 20), and an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis that counts missing drafts as zero (Table 11).

Every analysis is labelled pre-specified, post hoc or exploratory, and every post hoc choice is listed (Sec. 3.3 (a)-(i); Tables 2-3). This includes the symmetric completion rule, which was adopted after a first analysis put the evidence graph 2.1 points below direct reading (App. M.4). This level of transparency is rare and valuable.

The completion problem caused by safety-filter stops is identified and handled explicitly. Without the symmetric rule, a one-call strategy loses a whole entry while a per-paper strategy loses one paper (Sec. 3.3, Table 5). Completion is reported as an outcome, and sensitivity to it is shown (Tables 11, 32).

The split by whether the supplied text states each fact (Table 19, Fig. 2b-c, Fig. 6) is a useful analytic device. It shows that strategy differences live in a small headroom (about 4% of facts were stated but not fully conveyed, Sec. 4.1) and locates the case table's deficit in stated full-text facts (-8.4 points, Fig. 3a).

The audit stress test gives concrete, actionable evidence on a common design choice. Under the best-verdict-over-cited-papers rule, 0/30 added irrelevant citations were flagged, although the added paper's own per-paper verdict was 'unsupported' for all 176 attributed claims (Sec. 4.5, Table 50). Zygosity and 'one family' deletions were never caught (Table 51).

The memorisation control by creation date is informative. From the header alone, the memory-only control names the causal gene with F1 88.9-100% for older bands but 41.2% for the newest band and 30% for 2026 entries (Table 16, Fig. 5, App. M.2), and recall-then-verify shows how little memory content survives verification (Table 1).
Costs, call counts, stopped replies and deviations from planned designs are reported in detail (Tables 12, 34, 37-39, 48-49; App. J-L). Drafts, verdicts and per-entry scores are to be released.
Weaknesses: No human validation of any judgement. Fact splitting, present/partial/absent judging, the 'stated in the supplied text' judgement and the audit are all done by the same model family that writes the drafts (Sec. 4 preamble; Limitation (i)). The only reliability evidence is self-consistency: 95.7% per-fact agreement between two judgings (App. E). For a benchmark paper this is the central gap. The 1-3 point strategy and reading-better differences (Tables 1, 30) are of a size that judge bias or self-preference could produce. Even a few hundred facts labelled by geneticists, with chance-corrected agreement, would substantially strengthen the paper.

A single proprietary writer, run through a CLI with no temperature or seed control, also serves as judge (Sec. 3.2, App. B). Whether the access effect and the order of strategies transfer to other model families, especially smaller-context models where single-prompt reading is not possible, is untested (Limitation (ii)). The same model's safety filter removed entries unevenly across strategies: 7 of 100 main entries, 10 of 30 entries created in 2026 for the case table, and every one of the 4 large entries (Tables 5, 55, 49). This shapes which entries are compared, for reasons the authors cannot see.

The benchmark cannot be reused as released. The fixed fact lists are not redistributed. A rebuilt reference must be split again, and how much a fresh split shifts levels was not measured. The per-draft split procedure already ran 2-5 points higher (Sec. 3.1 'Reuse', Table 6, Ethics and Reproducibility statements). Third parties therefore cannot score a new strategy against the reported numbers, which weakens contribution (1).

The regime tested structurally favours direct reading and leaves little room for strategies to differ. All papers fit one prompt, 81% are abstracts or titles, and reading strategies already convey 91-94% of stated facts (Table 19). The authors say so (Sec. 5), but the regimes where designs might separate could not be evaluated: the 4 large entries produced no comparable entry (App. K.2), the 30-75-reference tier is 'without findings' (App. M.1), and padding used unrelated papers that no strategy cited (App. K.1). The headline conclusion that strategy matters little next to access is therefore narrow. It also rests on one implementation per paradigm (Limitation (iii)).

The primary endpoint is recall-only and narrow. It covers variant-centred ClinVar-deposited OMIM paragraphs, and only about 24% of a direct-reading draft's statements have a counterpart in them (App. H). The reading-better gains come with much longer drafts: 10,802 to 14,412 characters and 129 to 164 checkable claims for the completeness pass (Table 34). No length-controlled endpoint is reported (Limitation (iv)). The only precision-side check is the same-model audit on 20 entries, without intervals (Table 33). The three-draft merge's gain includes unsupported content (Table 30, 'not stated' +1.5; lower variant precision).

Much of the interesting evidence is post hoc or exploratory: the stated/not-stated restrictions (including the -8.4 point case-table result), the matched ablation, the stopped-entry sensitivity, the fourth reading-better arm, the planted-error classes and the released systems (Sec. 3.3, Tables 2-3). The confirmatory core consists of the main comparison (essentially null), the access experiment (expected, as the authors note in Sec. 1) and three prompt-level reading-better arms. The completeness-pass gain disappears on the mean when lost entries count as zero (-3.5, -11.1 to +2.6; Table 32), so the gain depends on a fallback rule.

Novelty and significance for an ML venue are limited. The strategies are prompt-level instances of known designs, and the paper explicitly contributes no new method (Sec. 2). The main findings are largely what one would predict: full text beats abstracts for variant facts, an attribution audit cannot see omissions, and best-verdict aggregation hides over-citation. The careful measurement is the contribution, but its reach is limited by the single model, the unvalidated judge and the non-redistributable reference.

The released-pipeline comparison adds little and risks being read as a ranking. It covers 10 and 4 entries. PaperQA2 ran without its agent, STORM produced no article because every chain-of-thought prompt was stopped, and the question-answering systems answered six concatenated questions while the strategies wrote a one-pass entry, which confounds protocol with design (App. J, Tables 35-43; Limitation (xii)).

Presentation is very dense. The main text is a sequence of hedged numerical statements with 55 appendix tables behind it. Key terms (stated, like for like, symmetric rule, completes, held out) are used in Sec. 1 before they are defined in Sec. 3.3. No worked example appears anywhere (curator paragraph -> fixed fact list -> draft paragraph -> per-fact judgement and audit verdict), which makes it hard to see what a 'fact' or 'partly present' is. Some set definitions need checking against tables. For example, it is unclear whether the 2,120 facts of the hidden-full-text experiment are only those of paragraphs about the hidden papers (Sec. 4.1 vs Table 24 vs Table 13).

There is a development/evaluation overlap and residual memorisation. The main strategies were developed on their evaluation entries (Limitation (ix)). Within abstract-only papers, direct reading's coverage falls from 49.8% (600000 band) to 37.9% (newest band) (Table 15). Of partly conveyed abstract-only facts, 10.0% are stated in no supplied text (Table 18). So reading is not shown to be free of recall, and the authors leave this unanalysed (Sec. 4.2).
Questions: Can you add a human validation on a stratified sample? For example, 200-300 fixed facts judged present/partly/absent by two clinical geneticists, plus the 'stated / not stated' label for the same facts, with Cohen's kappa against the model judge. Report it separately for full-text and abstract-only papers and for facts on which strategies disagree.

Can you re-judge a subset with a judge from another model family (for example, the 30 replicate entries of App. E) to test self-preference and correlated errors between the 'stated' and 'conveyed' judgements? Can you also run one other writer to see whether the 43.7-point access effect and the strategy order hold?

For reuse: can you estimate how much a fresh split by the same procedure moves levels and paired differences, for example by re-splitting the 30 replicate entries twice? Is there any route, such as an agreement with OMIM, to make the fixed fact lists available to other researchers?

In the hidden-full-text experiment, are the 2,120 facts restricted to paragraphs about the 91 hidden papers, or do they include facts about the abstract-only papers of the same entries? What is the effect on the hidden papers' facts alone?

Can you report a length-controlled comparison for the reading-better arms, for example coverage at matched characters or claims, or drafts truncated to baseline length, and a precision-side estimate with intervals on more than 20 entries?

What kinds of facts does the case table lose on stated full-text facts (-8.4 points, Fig. 3a)? For instance, does the per-patient schema drop functional-study or non-patient variant findings? Why is the evidence graph ahead on full-text facts (+1.2, Table 13) but behind on abstract facts (-1.9)?
Is there a time-stamped protocol (for example, a registered analysis plan) that documents which analyses were pre-specified before results were seen?
Are safety-filter stops concentrated in particular disease areas or paper types? Does excluding the 7 incomplete entries shift the compared set toward specific topics or creation eras?
Since the agentic curator's tool calls are not logged and paper opening is self-reported (App. B), how confident can one be that it read every paper, and could tool-call logging be added?
Limitations: The authors list limitations extensively and specifically (Sec. 5 (i)-(xii), Ethics statement): no human validation, one model family, few-reference regime, recall-only endpoint, a narrow and non-redistributable reference, open-access text only without supplements, and development on evaluation entries. These are the right limitations.

Not resolved within the paper, and the main threats to the conclusions: the absence of any human-labelled judge validation, of any second model family as writer or judge, and of a measurement of fresh-split stability for anyone rebuilding the reference.

The practical takeaway (access matters more than strategy) is specific to a variant-centred endpoint, to entries whose papers fit one prompt, and to one model whose safety filter removes entries non-randomly. These boundaries should be stated more prominently in the abstract and conclusion.

On societal impact, the paper notes that generated entries are drafts and must not be presented as OMIM content, and that a passed audit does not check correctness or completeness. Given the clinical-genetics setting, automation bias deserves a further sentence: reviewers may over-trust audited drafts when omissions and over-citation go undetected (Sec. 4.5).
